tweets.text: I Just Wrote the Brief That Will Take Down the SEC’s Crypto Deregulation Rule. It's Free. Cut. Paste. File. Win. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's proposed "Regulation Crypto Assets" (File No. S7-2026-27) would strip SEC registration protections from a fraud-saturated, multi-trillion-dollar so-called asset class. But peel back the white papers and the “asset” is math with a marketing budget: unsolvable equations spinning inside servers, producing nothing but the next number in the sequence. A colleague and I are hard at work on a mammoth comment letter. Stay tuned. But let’s be honest about the comment process. Comments are due 60 days after Federal Register publication. There's little suspense about whose views will actually count. Just look at the SEC's proposed rule eliminating quarterly-reporting: more than 200,000 Americans wrote in, and 99.5% said no, the most lopsided public rebuke of a rule-making in the agency’s 92-year history. Yet SEC Chairman Paul Atkins decided that the authors of the comment letters were all “confused.” Atkins doesn't care about comments. So in the meantime, here's something built to be filed, not filed away: My brief. My Brief. This is not a template. It's a cut-and-paste job. Every page (all 88), every word (all 20,000) and every footnote (all 138) is done. Any injured petitioner (investor, firm or state regulator) need only fill in the caption and file. My brief demonstrates that this Atkins debacle is unlawful five times over, because the SEC's proposed rule: 1️⃣ Exceeds the SEC’s exemptive authority under Securities Act Section 28 and Exchange Act Section 36, statutes now read de novo because Chevron is dead; 2️⃣ Rests on findings the record cannot support and the SEC’s own decade of litigated positions squarely contradicts; 3️⃣ Disregards the reliance interests that record created; 4️⃣ Cannot be sustained by any honest economic analysis; and 5️⃣ Arrogates to the SEC a decision of vast economic and political significance that belongs to Congress, which is actively considering, and has declined to enact, precisely the regime the Atkins Proposal would decree. The Stark Reality. Big Crypto has billions of dollars and an army of lobbyists. But they can't disappear the record, the case law and Article III Judges. In almost 40 years of SEC work and 20 years teaching at Georgetown and Duke Law, I've learned to be skeptical of anyone who promises a litigation result. But the strength here is the facts, the paper trail and the precedent, which leave the SEC with nowhere to stand. So, consider this my Joe Namath moment: The SEC's chances of winning a battle over its proposed "Regulation Crypto Assets" are slim and none -- and Slim just left town. If this SEC rule is adopted and challenged, the SEC will lose. Guaranteed. Download my brief at: https://t.co/NMckhIZHeR

tweets.text: RT @ProtonPrivacy: Recently, OpenAI shipped a plugin that lets ChatGPT read your Mac's Messages app, search it, and draft and send replies. However, this feature essentially renders Apple's end-to-end encryption obsolete, because your messages are now sitting on OpenAI's servers in plaintext. The plugin needs Full Disk Access, Contacts and Automation. If you have Messages in iCloud switched on, that's potentially years of history, attachments and identities, plus every SMS 2FA code your iPhone forwards to your Mac. OpenAI says it runs locally and doesn't build an index. Local execution isn't the same as local processing. The moment ChatGPT summarises a thread or drafts a reply using a hosted model, that content leaves the machine. In 2025 a US court ordered OpenAI to preserve ChatGPT conversations for the NYT case, including ones people had deleted. Under the CLOUD Act, data in OpenAI's control is reachable by US legal process wherever it's stored, and they can be barred from telling you it happened. Governments have spent a decade demanding a backdoor into iMessage and getting refused. This one installs itself, for free, with a toggle. If you've enabled it, everyone who has ever texted you is in it, and none of them know. Source @Paul__Walsh: https://t.co/eUJ6Vsvgkx

tweets.text: RT @Paul__Walsh: I’ve just spent hours responding to an avalanche of comments about the ChatGPT plugin for Apple Messages. Here are the main ones: 💬 "Anyone can screenshot your messages" Yes. They can also print them and fax them to the FBI. People using end to end encryption accept the risk that another participant can deliberately betray their trust. They don’t expect that person to give third party software ongoing access to read, search and analyse their private conversations. 💬 "I opted in, so it’s not a problem" You opted in. Everyone you communicate with didn’t. 💬 "The encryption still works, so you’re wrong" Yes, the cryptography still works. My concern is third party access to the readable content before or after decryption. 💬 "The recipient could always share your messages" Yes. The recipient could betray your trust. That doesn’t justify automating third party access to your private conversations. 💬 "Any Mac app with Full Disk Access could already do this" Yes. Apple specifically warns that Full Disk Access can expose Messages. OpenAI has now productised that capability for ordinary people who aren't aware of the potential implications, at scale. I don't think Apple saw this coming. 💬 "This is no different from giving AI access to email, SMS, Slack or Teams" It is. Those services don’t provide the same end to end encryption model as iMessage. Think Signal, not SMS. This Proton, not Gmail. The screenshot one is my favourite. I’ll either update my original article with an FAQ or write a dedicated follow up. Thankfully, these comments represent less than 2% of the responses I’ve received here. I haven’t even looked at LinkedIn yet. My concern with this implementation is scale. One person can enable it on their Mac and expose accessible conversations involving potentially hundreds of people who never enabled ChatGPT, never agreed to the access and aren’t notified. Depending on their Apple and iCloud configuration, that can include historical conversations, participant identifiers, contact information and attachments. Proton summarised my argument well after reading the article. I recommend reading their post first, then clicking through to mine for the full analysis. My Substack is free. I’m building a community around corporate surveillance, government overreach, privacy and personal digital safety. I’m interested in what the technology can do, what information it can access, who else can be affected and what happens when that capability is deployed at scale.

tweets.text: RT @matty_: Perps are a great tool to trade imminent IPOs, but a terrible tool to trade private names far-from-IPO date. The root problem is structural to private markets - it can't be solved by an oracle price or more speculative liquidity. Because unlike public/liquid underlyings, in private markets no hedge exists, and expected future appreciation is substantially positive and highly discrete. This means anyone going short must be *heavily* compensated for the systemic upside in these high-demand, constrained-supply names they are shorting. That's the reason ANTH-USDC perps are currently 45% premium to the OTC market, and 32% premium to @PreStocks Anthropic, not to mention the cost and uncertainty of variable funding rates on top of that. There's no free-lunch, only tradeoffs. Wider access means either: i) taking more vehicle/regulatory risk; ii) redistributing access from VCs to value-add individual investors (merit-based access); or iii) paying a higher premium
